Learning Objectives
Review the various conditions resulting in inflammatory arthritis.
Describe the unique preoperative evaluations necessary for patients with inflammatory
arthritis and the manner in which to optimize medical conditions to reduce surgical risks.
Review the perioperative management of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs.
Explain common surgical problems in the management of inflammatory hip disease and the
manner in which to prevent them.
Describe the most common complications after total hip arthroplasty in patients with
inflammatory arthritis and the manner in which to manage them.

Inflammatory Arthritis
Inflammatory arthritis and rheumatic disease are generic terms given to a large group of
different medical diagnoses and conditions that lead to inflammation and destruction of the
synovial joints. Inflammatory arthritis affects individuals of all ages and ethnic groups. Various
conditions have predilections for different ages and sexes. For example, rheumatoid arthritis
can occur at any age; however, its prevalence increases with age, and its peak incidence is in
individuals in their thirties to fifties.1 Other conditions, such as psoriatic arthritis and
seronegative spondyloarthropathies, frequently are associated with specific inflammatory
conditions of the skin and gut that require special attention in considering surgical
management. A great deal of flux exists in the nomenclature of the various inflammatory
arthropathies, and a detailed description of such is outside the goals of this discussion.
Rheumatoid Arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common inflammatory arthritis, with an estimated
prevalence of 0.5% to 1% in the United States.2 Rheumatoid arthritis is twice as common in
women as men. Genetics, environmental exposures, and lifestyle choices appear to contribute
to the pathogenesis of rheumatoid arthritis.
Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the current preferred terminology for the group of
inflammatory conditions presenting in children younger than 16 years and persisting for more
than 6 weeks with an unknown etiology. Previous terminology included juvenile rheumatoid
arthritis in the United States and juvenile chronic arthritis in Europe.
Oligoarticular JIA is the most common subtype of JIA. It is diagnosed in children in whom four
or fewer joints are involved. It is four times more common in girls and has a predilection for
larger joints. Uveitis is present in 20% of children.
Polyarticular JIA is diagnosed if a child has more than five joints involved. Children may have
a positive or a negative rheumatoid factor test. Uveitis is less common, and a predilection for
smaller joints exists.
Systemic JIA is the currently preferred term for patients in whom Still disease was previously
diagnosed. It is the least common subtype and often presents acutely with accompanying
rash. Systemic JIA must be differentiated from infection.

Preoperative Considerations
Medical evaluation
Rheumatic disease activity
Patients with inflammatory arthropathy should delay elective surgical treatment until their
systemic disease is well controlled.
Cardiac evaluation
Several inflammatory conditions are associated with an increased risk of cardiac disease.
Cardiovascular disease is a major contributor to increased mortality among patients with
rheumatoid arthritis, and it appears to be an independent risk factor for the development
of coronary heart disease. Risk assessment frequently is complicated by physical disability
and lack of mobility.
Vasculitis
Patients with vasculitis are at risk for renal, ocular, skin, neurologic, and vascular
complications. Evidence of vasculitis should be aggressively managed before elective
surgery.
Musculoskeletal evaluation
Inflammatory arthropathy can affect any synovial joint. A detailed patient history and
physical examination should be performed, with attention to gait, range of motion, and limb-
length inequality.
Contractures are common in patients with inflammatory arthritis and may result in
functional limb-length inequalities.
Deformities of the hindfoot and knee may have profound effects on the outcome of total hip
arthroplasty (THA) and should be closely evaluated. In general, deformities of the hindfoot
should be corrected before arthroplasty of the hip or knee. Hip arthroplasty can be
performed before knee arthroplasty, unless severe deformity is present.
Patients with symptomatic hip disease also may have problems with the axial skeleton in
addition to the other large joints. Specifically, the cervical spine should be evaluated for
atlantoaxial instability. Patients frequently are asymptomatic and may only be identified via
flexion-extension lateral cervical radiographs. Unidentified atlantoaxial instability may result
in catastrophic neurologic injury or death during endotracheal intubation. Intubation also
may be complicated by micrognathia, laryngomalacia, or temporomandibular joint disease.
These patients should be evaluated by an anesthesiologist before elective surgery.
Contractures of the upper extremity joints as a result of inflammatory disease may have
implications for positioning during hip arthroplasty and should be carefully assessed.

Medication management
A paucity of data exists to direct the management of the most common medications used to
treat patients with inflammatory arthritis. Concerns regarding wound healing and infection
have led to wide variability in clinical practice. A recent collaboration between the American
College of Rheumatology and the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons resulted in
a guideline for the perioperative management of antirheumatic medications in patients
undergoing elective hip and knee arthroplasty.3
Glucocorticoids
The current recommendation is to continue glucocorticoid therapy and the normal dose
through the perioperative period.
No evidence shows that supraphysiologic doses are necessary in patients with
inflammatory arthritis who are stable on low-dose glucocorticoids.
Low-dose glucocorticoids do not appear to substantially increase the risk of surgical site
infections; however, limited data shows that doses exceeding 15 mg of prednisone
equivalent per day are associated with an increased risk of periprosthetic joint infection.4
Nonbiologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs
Evidence appears to support continued therapy with methotrexate, leflunomide,
hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, and doxycycline.5
Biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs
The consensus for this class of drugs is to schedule surgery at the beginning of the dosing
cycle and withhold the medication for 1 to 2 weeks postoperatively.
The American College of Rheumatology/American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons
guideline made specific mention of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and defined it as
either severe or not severe. The recommendation was to continue mycophenolate,
azathioprine, cyclosporine, or tacrolimus in patients with severe SLE; however, those drugs
should be withheld for 1 week in patients without severe SLE.
Surgical Considerations
Preoperative planning
Preoperative planning is imperative in patients with inflammatory arthritis. Patients with JIA
frequently require small implants. Appropriate templating will ensure that appropriately
sized implants are available. Several inflammatory arthropathies are associated with
protrusio acetabuli6 (Figure 1; Resource 1).

The risk of infection with total joint arthroplasty is increased in patients with psoriatic
arthritis; therefore, skin incisions through active psoriatic lesions should be avoided because
of high bacterial colonization in such lesions.

Intraoperative considerations
Exposure
In patients with autofusion, or extreme stiffness, a trochanteric osteotomy may be
considered to facilitate acetabular exposure.
An incidence of nonunion approaching 20% has been reported with conventional
trochanteric osteotomy; a trochanteric slide or extended trochanteric osteotomy may be
considered a viable alternative to enhance exposure.
An in situ femoral neck osteotomy may be necessary in patients with severe protrusio
acetabuli to facilitate dislocation of the femoral head.
Acetabular reconstruction
Osteopenia and protrusio acetabuli frequently are encountered during THA for inflammatory
arthritis. Preoperative radiographs will demonstrate both conditions, and the surgeon can be
prepared for this finding. Medial bone grafting is a useful technique to restore bone stock
and reestablish the anatomic hip center6,7 (Figure 2). The resected femoral head provides
ample cancellous graft and can be morcellized with the use of a bone mill or acetabular
reamers8 (Figure 3; Resource 2).

Femoral reconstruction
Cemented and cementless components have been used successfully in patients with
inflammatory arthropathies; cementless components are the components most used to
date. 
Patients with inflammatory arthritis frequently have osteopenia and osteoporosis. This
decreased bone mineral density may increase the risk of intraoperative periprosthetic
fracture. The surgeon should be mindful of this risk and use cemented femoral implants if
decreased bone density is encountered.
THA in ankylosing spondylitis
Fixed pelvic hyperextension and loss of lumbar lordosis may lead to excessive functional
anteversion of the acetabular implant if a patient assumes an erect posture.
Excessive acetabular implant anteversion may increase the risk of anterior hip dislocation.
Placement of the acetabular implant in a more horizontal position with less anteversion
based on intraoperative pelvic landmarks—such as the anterior pelvic plane—is a method to
compensate for the fixed lumbopelvic deformity, improving the functional position of the
acetabular implant and avoiding anterior dislocation9 (Figure 4; Resource 3).

which gives the radiograph the appearance of an outlet view. Note the elongated obturator

for the fixed pelvic deformity. This positioning reduces the likelihood of anterior hip dislocation.

Complications
A recent analysis of the Nationwide Inpatient Sample was performed to compare perioperative
complications after THA in patients with inflammatory arthritis to those in patients with
osteoarthritis.10 Patients with inflammatory arthritis had a higher rate of postoperative
medical and orthopaedic complications. Specifically, patients with JIA had the highest risk of
orthopaedic complications overall and the highest risk of periprosthetic fracture. Rheumatoid
arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis were associated with an increased risk of wound
dehiscence. Patients with SLE had a substantially increased risk of mortality.
Infections

Many studies have investigated the risk of infection after hip or knee arthroplasty in patients
with inflammatory arthritis. Most studies evaluating this specific complication have focused
more on rheumatoid arthritis; however, some studies have attempted to evaluate all patients
with inflammatory arthritis. A 2008 study of 657 hip and knee arthroplasty implants reported
a 3.7% infection rate at a follow-up of 4 years, with a hazard ratio of 4.08 for rheumatoid
arthritis versus osteoarthritis.11 The incidence of periprosthetic joint infection in primary and
revision hips also was almost 3.7%. A 2012 meta-analysis reported that patients with
rheumatoid arthritis had a greater risk of periprosthetic joint infection and early revision
relative to patients with osteoarthritis.12
Dislocation
Several studies have identified rheumatoid arthritis as an independent risk factor for early
and late instability after THA.13,14
Outcomes
Most studies evaluating the functional outcomes of THA focus on patients with osteoarthritis.
Inflammatory arthritis includes a more complex subset of patients who span a wide range of
ages and functional status, making it difficult to draw conclusions.
Several studies have evaluated relatively small cohorts of patients with a single diagnosis and
have reported typically good results. A 2015 study examining the outcomes of 56 patients with
JIA found that Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Scores were favorable, and implant
survivorship at a follow-up of 10 years was 85%.15 Better implant survival was reported in
patients older than 25 years at the time of THA, and better outcome scores were reported in
men compared to women.
Conclusions
Patients with inflammatory arthritis present unique challenges that require thoughtful
preoperative planning and evaluation.
A team approach, consisting of an arthroplasty surgeon, rheumatologist, and anesthesiologist,
can produce safe and reproducible outcomes comparable to those of patients with
osteoarthritis.
